## 5. The normal form theorem

**Theorem 5.1 (Left transitivity).** $M$ is a sharp maximizer if and only if $M = U\Phi$ for some $U\in U(2)$.

*Proof.* ($\Rightarrow$) Put $U = \sqrt2 M$, unitary by Theorems 4.2 and 4.4. Then $U\Phi = \sqrt2 M\cdot\tfrac1{\sqrt2}I = M$. ($\Leftarrow$) $\Phi$ is a sharp maximizer (Theorem 4.4) and $M\mapsto UM = \Lambda_{U,I}(M)$ preserves sharpness (Theorem 2.11). $\square$

**Theorem 5.2 (Local-unitary normal form).** $M$ is a sharp maximizer if and only if there exist $U, V \in U(2)$ with
$$M \;=\; U\,\Phi\,V^{\mathsf T}.$$
Equivalently, the set of sharp maximizers is exactly the orbit of $\Phi$ under $U(2)\times U(2)$.

*Proof.* ($\Rightarrow$) Theorem 5.1 with $V = I$. ($\Leftarrow$) Theorem 2.11 applied to the sharp maximizer $\Phi$. $\square$

**Theorem 5.3 (Right transitivity).** $M$ is a sharp maximizer if and only if $M = \Phi V^{\mathsf T}$ for some $V \in U(2)$.

*Proof.* Since $\Phi$ is a scalar matrix it commutes with every matrix. Given a sharp maximizer, Theorem 5.1 provides $U$ with $M = U\Phi = \Phi U$; take $V = U^{\mathsf T}$, unitary by Lemma 2.10, so that $V^{\mathsf T} = U$. The converse is Theorem 2.11 again. $\square$

**Corollary 5.4 (Transitivity on the orbit).** If $M$ and $N$ are sharp maximizers then $N = WM$ for some $W\in U(2)$.

*Proof.* Write $M = A\Phi$ and $N = B\Phi$ with $A,B$ unitary (Theorem 5.1) and set $W = BA^{\dagger}$, which is unitary. Then $WM = BA^{\dagger}A\Phi = B\Phi = N$. $\square$

Corollary 5.4 says that a *single-sided* local rotation suffices to convert any maximally entangled state into any other — an operationally meaningful statement, since it means one party acting alone can perform the conversion.

**Theorem 5.5 (Stabilizer of the Bell state).** Let $U \in U(2)$ and let $V$ be any matrix. Then
$$U\,\Phi\,V^{\mathsf T} = \Phi \iff V = \overline{U},$$
where $\overline U = (U^{\dagger})^{\mathsf T}$ is the entrywise complex conjugate of $U$. Thus the stabilizer of $\Phi$ in $U(2)\times U(2)$ is $\{(U,\overline U) : U \in U(2)\}$, a copy of $U(2)$.

*Proof.* Since $\Phi = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}I$ is scalar, $U\Phi V^{\mathsf T} = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}\,UV^{\mathsf T}$, so the equation is equivalent to $UV^{\mathsf T} = I$ after cancelling the nonzero scalar. Multiplying on the left by $U^{\dagger}$ and using $U^{\dagger}U = I$ gives $V^{\mathsf T} = U^{\dagger}$, i.e. $V = (U^{\dagger})^{\mathsf T} = \overline U$. Conversely if $V = \overline U$ then $V^{\mathsf T} = U^{\dagger}$ and $UV^{\mathsf T} = UU^{\dagger} = I$. $\square$

Theorem 5.5 quantifies the freedom in the normal form: the orbit is $\bigl(U(2)\times U(2)\bigr)/U(2)$, of real dimension $4 + 4 - 4 = 4$; taking into account the global phase, which acts trivially on physical states, the maximizers form a $4$-real-dimensional family of matrices inside the $7$-sphere of normalized states.

**Corollary 5.6 (Extremes are disjoint).** A sharp maximizer is never a product state.

*Proof.* A product state has $C = 0$ by Theorem 2.13, while a sharp maximizer has $C = 1$. $\square$

## 6. Flat maximizers and complex Hadamard matrices of order two

**Definition 6.1.** $M$ is *flat* if $|m_{ij}| = \tfrac12$ for all $i,j$. Write
$$F_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}$$
for the order-two Fourier (Hadamard) matrix.

A flat sharp maximizer, rescaled by $2$, is exactly a *complex Hadamard matrix* of order two: a matrix with unimodular entries and pairwise orthogonal rows.

**Lemma 6.2.** If $d = (d_0,d_1)$ with $|d_i| = 1$, then $\operatorname{diag}(d)$ is unitary. Moreover $\tfrac12 F_2$ is a flat sharp maximizer.

*Proof.* $\operatorname{diag}(d)\operatorname{diag}(d)^{\dagger} = \operatorname{diag}(|d_0|^2, |d_1|^2) = I$. For $F_2$: $(\tfrac12F_2)(\tfrac12F_2)^{\dagger} = \tfrac14 F_2F_2^{\mathsf T} = \tfrac14\cdot 2I = \tfrac12 I$, so Theorem 4.3 applies; flatness is immediate. $\square$

**Theorem 6.3 (Dephasing).** Let $M$ be a flat sharp maximizer. Then there exist unimodular vectors $d, e \in \mathbb{C}^2$ with
$$M \;=\; \operatorname{diag}(d)\,\bigl(\tfrac12 F_2\bigr)\,\operatorname{diag}(e).$$

*Proof.* Flatness gives $m_{ij}\overline{m_{ij}} = \tfrac14$ for all $i,j$, and in particular every entry is nonzero. The orthogonality relation of Theorem 4.1 reads $m_{00}\overline{m_{10}} + m_{01}\overline{m_{11}} = 0$. Multiply it by $4 m_{10}m_{11}$ and substitute $4m_{10}\overline{m_{10}} = 1$, $4m_{11}\overline{m_{11}} = 1$, obtaining the *unconjugated* relation
$$m_{00}m_{11} + m_{01}m_{10} = 0. \tag{6.1}$$
Now take $d = \bigl(1,\; m_{10}/m_{00}\bigr)$ and $e = \bigl(2m_{00},\,2m_{01}\bigr)$; both are unimodular by flatness. The product $\operatorname{diag}(d)(\tfrac12 F_2)\operatorname{diag}(e)$ has entries
$$\begin{pmatrix} m_{00} & m_{01} \\ m_{10} & -m_{01}m_{10}/m_{00}\end{pmatrix},$$
and the bottom-right entry equals $m_{11}$ precisely by (6.1). $\square$

**Theorem 6.4 (Flat classification).** $M$ is a flat sharp maximizer if and only if $M = \operatorname{diag}(d)\,(\tfrac12 F_2)\,\operatorname{diag}(e)$ for unimodular $d, e$.

*Proof.* ($\Rightarrow$) Theorem 6.3. ($\Leftarrow$) Sharpness follows from Lemma 6.2 and Theorem 2.11 (note $\operatorname{diag}(e) = \operatorname{diag}(e)^{\mathsf T}$, so this is a legitimate local action); flatness is a direct computation on the four entries, each of which is $\pm\tfrac12 d_i e_j$. $\square$

This is the order-two case of the classification of complex Hadamard matrices, and it is a *rigidity* statement: whereas the full maximizer set requires the six-parameter group $U(2)\times U(2)$ (modulo stabilizer) to sweep out, the flat locus requires only the three-parameter torus of diagonal phases (four phases modulo one global phase). There is no continuous family of order-two complex Hadamard matrices beyond dephasing — the *defect* is zero. (Contrast order four, where a genuine one-parameter family exists.)

### 6.1 The real count

**Definition 6.5.** For $a,b,c,d \in \{\pm\}$ let $S(a,b,c,d)$ be the matrix with entries $\pm\tfrac12$ according to the four signs.

**Theorem 6.6 (Sign criterion).** $S(a,b,c,d)$ is a sharp maximizer if and only if the propositions "$a = d$" and "$b = c$" have opposite truth values.

*Proof.* Every such matrix is automatically normalized, since $4\cdot\tfrac14 = 1$. Its determinant is $\tfrac14(ad - bc)$ with $ad, bc \in \{\pm1\}$, so $|\det| = \tfrac12$ iff $ad = -bc$, i.e. iff exactly one of $ad = 1$, $bc = 1$ holds. $\square$

**Corollary 6.7 (The count).** Exactly $8$ of the $16$ real sign patterns are sharp maximizers.

*Proof.* Condition on $ad$: for each of the $8$ pairs $(a,d)$ there are exactly $2$ pairs $(b,c)$ with $bc = -ad$ out of $4$; more simply, the map $(a,b,c,d)\mapsto(a,b,c,-d)$ is a fixed-point-free involution exchanging the maximizers with the non-maximizers, so the two classes have equal size $8$. $\square$

Equivalently, the $8$ real maximizers form a single orbit of the sign group $\{\pm1\}^3$ (row signs and column signs modulo the global sign) through $\tfrac12 F_2$ — the real shadow of Theorem 6.4.

## 7. The Bell basis

Define the Hilbert–Schmidt inner product on amplitude matrices,
$$\langle M, N\rangle_{HS} = \sum_{i,j}\overline{m_{ij}}\,n_{ij},$$
which is the standard inner product of the corresponding state vectors. Let $\sigma_0 = I$ and
$$\sigma_x = \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y = \begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$$
be the Pauli matrices, and set $\Phi_k = \sigma_k\Phi = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}\sigma_k$ for $k \in \{0,x,y,z\}$.

**Lemma 7.1.** Each $\sigma_k$ is unitary, and $\langle \sigma_j,\sigma_k\rangle_{HS} = 2\,\delta_{jk}$.

*Proof.* Direct computation on $2\times2$ matrices; each $\sigma_k$ squares to $I$ and is Hermitian, and the four are pairwise Hilbert–Schmidt orthogonal with squared norm $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_k^2) = 2$. $\square$

**Theorem 7.2 (Bell basis).** The four states $\Phi_0, \Phi_x, \Phi_y, \Phi_z$ are sharp maximizers, are orthonormal for $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{HS}$, and form a basis: every amplitude matrix satisfies
$$M \;=\; \sum_{k} \langle \Phi_k, M\rangle_{HS}\;\Phi_k .$$

*Proof.* Sharpness: $\Phi_k = \Lambda_{\sigma_k, I}(\Phi)$ and $\sigma_k$ is unitary, so Theorem 2.11 applies. Orthonormality: $\langle \Phi_j, \Phi_k\rangle_{HS} = \tfrac12\langle\sigma_j,\sigma_k\rangle_{HS} = \delta_{jk}$ by Lemma 7.1. Completeness: the Pauli matrices span $\mathbb{C}^{2\times2}$ with the expansion $M = \tfrac12\sum_k\langle\sigma_k,M\rangle_{HS}\,\sigma_k$ (verify entrywise, or note that orthogonality plus a dimension count forces it), and substituting $\sigma_k = \sqrt2\,\Phi_k$ and $\langle\sigma_k,M\rangle_{HS} = \sqrt2\langle\Phi_k,M\rangle_{HS}$ yields the stated formula. $\square$

Theorem 7.2 is the structural fact behind superdense coding and teleportation: there exists an orthonormal basis of the four-dimensional two-qubit state space consisting *entirely* of maximally entangled states, and its members differ by a unitary acting on one side only.

---

## 8. Purity, linear entropy, and the Schmidt spectrum

Cayley–Hamilton in dimension two, $A^2 - (\operatorname{tr}A)A + (\det A)I = 0$, gives in trace form $\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = (\operatorname{tr}A)^2 - 2\det A$. Applying this to $\rho = MM^{\dagger}$ and using (2.1):

**Proposition 8.1.** $P(M) = \operatorname{tr}\rho^2 = \|M\|_F^4 - 2|\det M|^2$.

**Theorem 8.2 (Linear-entropy identity).** For every normalized $M$,
$$C(M)^2 \;=\; 2\bigl(1 - \operatorname{tr}\rho^2\bigr).$$

*Proof.* Put $\|M\|_F^2 = 1$ into Proposition 8.1: $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2 = 1 - 2|\det M|^2 = 1 - \tfrac12 C^2$. Rearrange. $\square$

The quantity $1 - \operatorname{tr}\rho^2$ is the *linear entropy* of the marginal; Theorem 8.2 says the squared concurrence is exactly twice it, so the two standard measures of entanglement for a two-qubit pure state — non-factorizability of the amplitude matrix, and mixedness of the marginal — are literally the same function up to a change of variable.

**Corollary 8.3 (Minimal purity).** Every normalized state has $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2 \ge \tfrac12$, and equality holds exactly at the sharp maximizers.

*Proof.* $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2 = 1 - \tfrac12C^2 \ge 1 - \tfrac12 = \tfrac12$ using $C \le 1$ (Theorem 3.4), with equality iff $C = 1$ (using $C \ge 0$). $\square$

### 8.1 The Schmidt spectrum

**Definition 8.4.** For a normalized state set
$$s_{\pm}(M) = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{1 - C(M)^2}}{2}.$$

**Lemma 8.5.** $s_+ + s_- = 1$, $s_+s_- = |\det M|^2$, and $0 \le s_- \le s_+ \le 1$.

*Proof.* The sum is immediate. For the product, $s_+s_- = \tfrac14\bigl(1 - (1-C^2)\bigr) = \tfrac14 C^2 = |\det M|^2$, using $\bigl(\sqrt{1-C^2}\bigr)^2 = 1 - C^2$, legitimate since $C \le 1$. The bounds follow from $0 \le \sqrt{1-C^2} \le 1$. $\square$

**Theorem 8.6 (Schmidt spectrum).** For a normalized state,
$$\bigl(\rho - s_+ I\bigr)\bigl(\rho - s_- I\bigr) = 0 .$$
Thus the eigenvalues of the marginal — the squared Schmidt coefficients of the state — are exactly $s_{\pm}(M)$.

*Proof.* Expand the left side as $\rho^2 - (s_++s_-)\rho + s_+s_-I = \rho^2 - (\operatorname{tr}\rho)\rho + (\det\rho)I$, using Lemma 8.5 with $\operatorname{tr}\rho = \|M\|_F^2 = 1$ and $\det\rho = |\det M|^2$. This vanishes by Cayley–Hamilton. $\square$

**Corollary 8.7 (Both extremes as spectral degeneracies).** For a normalized state:
1. $M$ is a sharp maximizer $\iff s_+ = s_-$ (spectrum $\{\tfrac12,\tfrac12\}$);
2. $M$ is a product state $\iff s_- = 0$ (spectrum $\{1,0\}$).

*Proof.* $s_+ - s_- = \sqrt{1-C^2}$, which vanishes iff $C^2 = 1$ iff $C = 1$ (as $C \ge 0$). And $2s_- = 1 - \sqrt{1-C^2}$ vanishes iff $\sqrt{1-C^2} = 1$ iff $C = 0$, which by Theorem 2.13 is the product condition. $\square$

The concurrence therefore interpolates monotonically between the two degeneracies of a one-parameter spectral family, and the classification of §4–5 is the statement that the *flat-spectrum* end of this family is a single group orbit.

## 9. Stability: a quantitative inverse theorem

The proof of Theorem 4.1 discarded a non-negative term; retaining it turns the classification into an exact identity, and hence into a robust statement.

**Lemma 9.1.** For every $M$,
$$\bigl\|\rho - \tfrac12 I\bigr\|_F^2 = \bigl(\|r_0\|^2 - \tfrac12\bigr)^2 + \bigl(\|r_1\|^2 - \tfrac12\bigr)^2 + 2\,\bigl|\langle r_0,r_1\rangle\bigr|^2 ,$$
where $\rho = MM^{\dagger}$.

*Proof.* The entries of $\rho$ are $\rho_{00} = \|r_0\|^2$, $\rho_{11} = \|r_1\|^2$, $\rho_{01} = \langle r_0,r_1\rangle$, $\rho_{10} = \overline{\rho_{01}}$. Subtract $\tfrac12 I$ and sum the four squared moduli. $\square$

**Theorem 9.2 (Exact stability identity).** For every normalized $M$,
$$\bigl\|\,MM^{\dagger} - \tfrac12 I\,\bigr\|_F^2 \;=\; \frac{1 - C(M)^2}{2}.$$

*Proof.* Write $x = \|r_0\|^2$, $y = \|r_1\|^2$, $t = |\langle r_0,r_1\rangle|^2$, $D = |\det M|^2 = C^2/4$. Normalization gives $x + y = 1$ and the Gram relation (3.1) gives $t + D = xy$. Then
$$\bigl(x-\tfrac12\bigr)^2 + \bigl(y-\tfrac12\bigr)^2 = \tfrac12 (x-y)^2 = \tfrac12\bigl((x+y)^2 - 4xy\bigr) = \tfrac12\bigl(1 - 4t - 4D\bigr),$$
so by Lemma 9.1 the left-hand side of the theorem equals $\tfrac12 - 2t - 2D + 2t = \tfrac12 - 2D = \tfrac12 - \tfrac{C^2}{2}$. $\square$

Note that the cross terms cancel exactly: the off-diagonal contribution $2t$ is precisely compensated by the $t$-dependence of the diagonal deficit. This is why the identity is clean.

**Corollary 9.3 (Deficit bound).** For every normalized $M$,
$$\bigl\|\,MM^{\dagger} - \tfrac12 I\,\bigr\|_F^2 \;\le\; 1 - C(M).$$

*Proof.* $\tfrac12(1-C^2) = \tfrac12(1-C)(1+C) \le (1-C)$ since $0 \le C \le 1$. $\square$

**Corollary 9.4.** For a normalized $M$, $\;\|MM^{\dagger} - \tfrac12 I\|_F = 0$ if and only if $M$ is a sharp maximizer.

Thus if a state's concurrence falls short of the maximum by $\varepsilon$, its marginal lies within Frobenius distance $\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ of the maximally mixed state, and the exponent $\tfrac12$ is optimal: the exact identity of Theorem 9.2 shows the distance is $\Theta(\sqrt{\varepsilon})$ as $\varepsilon\to0$ along a curve with $C = 1-\varepsilon$. The classification is therefore not a knife-edge phenomenon; it degrades continuously and with an explicit modulus.

## 10. Algorithmic content

The theory above is entirely constructive and yields short algorithms.

**Algorithm A (Certify maximality).** Given $M$, compute $\|M\|_F^2$ and $\det M$ in $O(1)$ arithmetic operations; report *sharp maximizer* iff $\|M\|_F^2 = 1$ and $2|\det M| = 1$. By Theorem 4.3 this is equivalent to the four-entry test $MM^{\dagger} = \tfrac12 I$, which is a useful cross-check and is what one measures experimentally (state tomography of one qubit).

**Algorithm B (Normal-form extraction).** Given a sharp maximizer $M$, return $U = \sqrt2\,M$ and $V = I$; then $M = U\Phi V^{\mathsf T}$ and $U$ is unitary (Theorem 4.4). Cost $O(1)$; the certificate can be verified by checking $UU^{\dagger} = I$.

**Algorithm C (Interconversion).** Given sharp maximizers $M, N$, return $W = 2\,N M^{\dagger}$. Indeed $W = (\sqrt2 N)(\sqrt2 M)^{\dagger}$ is a product of unitaries, hence unitary, and $WM = 2NM^{\dagger}M = 2N\cdot\tfrac12 I= N$ using $M^\dagger M = \tfrac12 I$ (which holds because $\sqrt2 M$ is unitary and unitaries satisfy $A^\dagger A = I$). This realizes Corollary 5.4 with an explicit $O(1)$ formula.

**Algorithm D (Dephasing a flat maximizer).** Given a flat sharp maximizer $M$, return $d = (1, m_{10}/m_{00})$ and $e = (2m_{00}, 2m_{01})$; then $M = \operatorname{diag}(d)(\tfrac12 F_2)\operatorname{diag}(e)$ by Theorem 6.3.

**Algorithm E (Bell-basis transform).** Given any $M$, return the four coefficients $c_k = \langle\Phi_k, M\rangle_{HS} = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_k^{\dagger}M)$; by Theorem 7.2, $M = \sum_k c_k\Phi_k$ and $\sum_k|c_k|^2 = \|M\|_F^2$. This is the $4$-point transform underlying Bell-basis measurement.

**Algorithm F (Schmidt spectrum).** Given a normalized $M$, return $s_{\pm} = \bigl(1\pm\sqrt{1-C^2}\bigr)/2$ with $C = 2|\det M|$; by Theorem 8.6 these are the eigenvalues of $MM^{\dagger}$, obtained without diagonalizing anything.

Every algorithm is $O(1)$ because the underlying dimension is fixed; the point is not complexity but that each theorem supplies an explicit witness, so the classification can be *used*, not merely quoted.

## 11. Discussion and applications

**Entanglement as an extremal problem.** The narrative of §3–5 is a template. A sharp inequality is proved by dropping one non-negative term and applying AM–GM; the equality case reinstates both, forcing two equations; those equations assemble into a matrix identity ($\rho = \tfrac12 I$); the matrix identity says the object is unitary after rescaling; and unitarity is precisely membership in a group orbit. Wherever this template applies — Hadamard matrices, tight frames, extremal graphs, isoperimetric problems — one expects the maximizer set to be a single orbit and the proof of the inequality, read backwards, to be the classification.

**Operational content.** Theorem 4.3 is the statement that maximal entanglement is *exactly* maximal local ignorance, which is why the halves of a Bell pair are individually useless: each is a uniformly random bit. Corollary 5.4 says either party can convert their shared maximally entangled state into any other by acting alone, which is why "maximally entangled state" is a resource without further qualification: there is only one, up to local relabelling. Theorem 5.5 explains the isotropy of Bell correlations: rotating one particle by $U$ can always be undone by rotating the other by $\overline U$. Theorem 7.2 is the mathematical substrate of superdense coding (four distinguishable messages encoded by one-sided Pauli operations) and teleportation (measurement in a maximally entangled basis).

**Combinatorial content.** Theorem 6.4 and Corollary 6.7 place the analysis in contact with the combinatorics of Hadamard matrices. Order two is the base case of a hierarchy that becomes hard fast: the classification of complex Hadamard matrices is complete only up to order five. What the base case exhibits cleanly is the phenomenon of *defect zero* — the only deformations of $F_2$ through complex Hadamard matrices are the trivial ones by row and column phases. The real count $8 = |\{\pm1\}^3|$ is a single orbit of the sign group, the exact discrete shadow of the torus statement.

**Stability.** Theorem 9.2 upgrades a rigidity theorem to a robustness theorem. In an experimental setting one never certifies $C = 1$; one certifies $C \ge 1 - \varepsilon$. Corollary 9.3 converts that certificate directly into a bound on how far the observed one-qubit marginal can be from maximally mixed — an inequality between two quantities that are separately measurable, with no free constants.

## 12. Future directions

**Direction 1 — A complete local-unitary invariant via the Schmidt normal form.** The row classification is the equality case of a Gram inequality whose *general* case is the singular value decomposition. The same Lagrange identity that produced $MM^{\dagger} = \tfrac12 I$ should produce the general normal form $M = U\operatorname{diag}(s,t)V^{\mathsf T}$, exhibiting the Schmidt coefficients of §8 as a complete invariant of the local action on *all* states, not just maximizers. The ingredients are in place: $MM^{\dagger}$ is Hermitian positive semidefinite with the spectrum computed in Theorem 8.6, the degenerate cases in dimension two are a finite check, and the orbit machinery of §2.2 already applies. The expected conclusion — that $|\det M|$ together with $\|M\|_F^2$ is a *complete* invariant of the two-sided action, so two states are locally equivalent iff they have the same concurrence — would place all of §4–9 inside a single classification.

**Direction 2 — The Hadamard defect and the rigidity of $F_2$.** Theorem 6.3 shows the order-two complex Hadamard matrices admit exactly a three-parameter dephasing group and no continuous family beyond it, i.e. defect zero; order four, by contrast, carries a genuine one-parameter family. A formal notion of *defect* — the dimension of the space of infinitesimal deformations preserving both unimodularity and orthogonality, modulo dephasing — would explain both facts uniformly, and the order-two case now provides a fully proved base case against which to calibrate the definition rather than folklore.

**Direction 3 — Sharpness stability: from marginal to state.** The equality-case argument only ever used the bound $|\langle r_0,r_1\rangle|^2 \le \varepsilon$, so it is already quantitative: one expects $\|M\|_F^2 - 2|\det M| \le \varepsilon$ to force $M$ to lie within Frobenius distance $O(\sqrt{\varepsilon})$ of the maximizer orbit. Theorem 9.2 supplies the marginal-level half of this exactly, in the form $\|\rho - \tfrac12 I\|_F^2 = (1-C^2)/2$. What remains is the passage from "marginal close to $\tfrac12 I$" to "state close to the orbit", i.e. a perturbative version of Theorem 4.4: if $MM^{\dagger}$ is within $\delta$ of $\tfrac12 I$, then $\sqrt2 M$ is within $O(\delta)$ of a unitary — a two-dimensional instance of the Lin-type problem of approximating almost-unitary matrices by unitary ones, where the polar decomposition should give the optimal constant.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The extremal problem}

Let $M\in\CC^{2\times2}$ have entries $m_{ij}$, $i,j\in\{0,1\}$. We regard $M$ as the amplitude
matrix of the pure two-qubit state
\[
  \lvert\psi_M\rangle \;=\; \sum_{i,j\in\{0,1\}} m_{ij}\,\lvert ij\rangle,
\]
so that $\lvert m_{ij}\rvert^2$ is the probability of the outcome $(i,j)$ and
$\Fro{M}^2=\sum_{i,j}\lvert m_{ij}\rvert^2$ is the total probability. The state is
\emph{normalized} when $\Fro{M}^2=1$. The question we answer completely is:

\begin{quote}
Among normalized amplitude matrices, which maximize $\lvert\det M\rvert$, and what is the geometry
of the maximizing set?
\end{quote}

This is not an idle question. As recalled in \S\ref{sec:product}, $\det M$ vanishes exactly on the
unentangled (product) states, so its modulus is a canonical measure of entanglement; twice it is
Wootters' \emph{concurrence} $C(M)=2\lvert\det M\rvert$.

The answers are: the maximum is $C=1$; the maximizing set is a single orbit of the group of local
unitaries; and every finer question one can ask about that orbit --- its stabilizer, its flat locus,
its relationship to orthonormal bases, its stability under perturbation --- has an explicit answer
obtained from the same two-line computation.

\subsection{Method}

The whole development rests on one classical identity. For $u=(a,b)$ and $v=(c,d)$ in $\CC^2$,
Lagrange's identity (the $2\times2$ case of Cauchy--Binet) states
\[
  \lvert\ip{u}{v}\rvert^2 + \lvert ad-bc\rvert^2 = \lVert u\rVert^2\,\lVert v\rVert^2,
  \qquad \ip{u}{v} = a\overline c + b\overline d .
\]
Applied to the two rows of $M$ this is the Gram relation
$\lvert\ip{r_0}{r_1}\rvert^2 + \lvert\det M\rvert^2 = \lVert r_0\rVert^2\lVert r_1\rVert^2$,
from which the sharp bound follows by AM--GM. Every classification statement below is the
\emph{equality case} of this single relation, and every quantitative statement is the identity read
with the error terms retained rather than discarded. That is the structural moral of the work: the
analytic content of ``maximal entanglement'' is one equality case of one classical identity.

\section{Definitions and the local group action}

\subsection{States and invariants}

\begin{definition}
An \emph{amplitude matrix} is a matrix $M\in\CC^{2\times2}$. Its \emph{squared Frobenius norm} is
$\Fro{M}^2=\sum_{i,j}\lvert m_{ij}\rvert^2$; it is \emph{normalized} when $\Fro{M}^2=1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{concurrence} of $M$ is $C(M)=2\lvert\det M\rvert$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
$M$ is a \emph{sharp maximizer} if it is normalized and $C(M)=1$.
\end{definition}

The terminology anticipates Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp}, which shows $C\le1$ on normalized states.

\begin{definition}
The \emph{Bell state} is $\Phi=\diag\bigl(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2\bigr)=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\Id$; as a state
vector, $\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\lvert 00\rangle+\lvert 11\rangle)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
Write $r_0=(m_{00},m_{01})$ and $r_1=(m_{10},m_{11})$ for the rows of $M$, and set
\[
  \lVert r_0\rVert^2 = \lvert m_{00}\rvert^2+\lvert m_{01}\rvert^2, \quad
  \lVert r_1\rVert^2 = \lvert m_{10}\rvert^2+\lvert m_{11}\rvert^2, \quad
  \ip{r_0}{r_1} = m_{00}\overline{m_{10}}+m_{01}\overline{m_{11}} .
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:rows}
$\Fro{M}^2 = \lVert r_0\rVert^2 + \lVert r_1\rVert^2$, and both summands are non-negative.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Expand the double sum by rows.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{marginal} (reduced density matrix of the first qubit) is $\rho=MM^{\dagger}$, and its
\emph{purity} is $\tr\rho^2$.
\end{definition}

Two identities are used repeatedly:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tracedet}
  \tr(MM^{\dagger}) = \Fro{M}^2, \qquad \det(MM^{\dagger}) = \lvert\det M\rvert^2 .
\end{equation}
The first is the row expansion again; the second follows from multiplicativity of $\det$ and
$\det(M^{\dagger}) = \overline{\det M}$.

\subsection{The local unitary action}

Local operations act on the two qubits independently. On amplitude matrices an operator $U\otimes V$
acts by left multiplication by $U$ and right multiplication by the \emph{transpose} of $V$; the
transpose arises because the second index of $M$ is a ket index contracted against $V$.

\begin{definition}
For $U,V\in\Ut$ set $L_U(M)=UM$, $R_V(M)=MV^{\mathsf T}$ and $\Lambda_{U,V}(M)=U M V^{\mathsf T}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Action laws]
$\Lambda_{U,V}=L_U\circ R_V$; $\Lambda_{\Id,\Id}=\mathrm{id}$; $L_{U_1U_2}=L_{U_1}\circ L_{U_2}$;
$R_{V_1V_2}=R_{V_1}\circ R_{V_2}$; and
$\Lambda_{U_1U_2,\,V_1V_2}=\Lambda_{U_1,V_1}\circ\Lambda_{U_2,V_2}$. Hence $\Lambda$ is a left
action of $\Ut\times\Ut$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Associativity of matrix multiplication, together with $(V_1V_2)^{\mathsf T}=V_2^{\mathsf T}V_1^{\mathsf T}$
and the right-hand placement of the transposed factor.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:closure}
If $V$ is unitary then so are $V^{\mathsf T}$ and $V^{\dagger}$, and $\lvert\det U\rvert=1$ for
unitary $U$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
From $V^{\dagger}V=\Id$ we get $V^{\mathsf T}(V^{\mathsf T})^{\dagger}=V^{\mathsf T}\overline V
=(V^{\dagger}V)^{\mathsf T}=\Id$. Unitarity of $V^{\dagger}$ is the definition read symmetrically.
Finally $\det U\cdot\overline{\det U}=\det(UU^{\dagger})=1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Invariance]\label{thm:inv}
For $U,V\in\Ut$ and any $M$,
\[
  \Fro{\Lambda_{U,V}(M)}^2=\Fro{M}^2,\qquad
  \lvert\det\Lambda_{U,V}(M)\rvert=\lvert\det M\rvert,\qquad
  C(\Lambda_{U,V}M)=C(M).
\]
In particular the local action preserves normalization and sharpness.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:closure},
$(UMV^{\mathsf T})(UMV^{\mathsf T})^{\dagger}=UMV^{\mathsf T}\overline V M^{\dagger}U^{\dagger}
=U(MM^{\dagger})U^{\dagger}$, and cyclicity of the trace with \eqref{eq:tracedet} gives the first
claim. For the second, $\det(UMV^{\mathsf T})=\det U\det M\det V$ and both unitary determinants are
unimodular.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Product states}\label{sec:product}

\begin{definition}
$M$ is a \emph{product state} if there exist $u,w\in\CC^2$ with $m_{ij}=u_iw_j$ for all $i,j$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:product}
$C(M)=0$ if and only if $M$ is a product state.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $m_{ij}=u_iw_j$ then $\det M=u_0w_0u_1w_1-u_0w_1u_1w_0=0$. Conversely suppose
$m_{00}m_{11}=m_{01}m_{10}$. If $m_{00}\neq0$, take $u=(1,m_{10}/m_{00})$ and $w=(m_{00},m_{01})$;
three entries match trivially and the fourth, $m_{10}m_{01}/m_{00}=m_{11}$, is exactly the
determinant condition. If $m_{00}=0$ and $m_{01}\neq0$, then $m_{01}m_{10}=0$ forces $m_{10}=0$ and
$u=(1,m_{11}/m_{01})$, $w=(m_{00},m_{01})$ works. If $m_{00}=m_{01}=0$, take $u=(0,1)$,
$w=(m_{10},m_{11})$.
\end{proof}

\section{The Gram relation and the sharp bound}

\begin{lemma}[Lagrange's identity in dimension two]\label{lem:lagrange}
For all $a,b,c,d\in\CC$,
\[
  \lvert a\overline c+b\overline d\rvert^2 + \lvert ad-bc\rvert^2
   = \bigl(\lvert a\rvert^2+\lvert b\rvert^2\bigr)\bigl(\lvert c\rvert^2+\lvert d\rvert^2\bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $a=a_1+ia_2$ and likewise for $b,c,d$ and expand both sides as real polynomials in the eight
real variables. All mixed terms on the left cancel and what survives is the expansion of
$(a_1^2+a_2^2+b_1^2+b_2^2)(c_1^2+c_2^2+d_1^2+d_2^2)$. Equivalently the identity is Cauchy--Binet for
the Gram determinant of the pair $\{(a,b),(c,d)\}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Gram relation]\label{cor:gram}
For every $M\in\CC^{2\times2}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gram}
  \lvert\ip{r_0}{r_1}\rvert^2+\lvert\det M\rvert^2 = \lVert r_0\rVert^2\lVert r_1\rVert^2 .
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:lagrange} with $(a,b)=(m_{00},m_{01})$, $(c,d)=(m_{10},m_{11})$, noting
$\det M=m_{00}m_{11}-m_{01}m_{10}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Hadamard's inequality in dimension two]\label{cor:hadamard}
$\lvert\det M\rvert^2\le\lVert r_0\rVert^2\lVert r_1\rVert^2$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp bound]\label{thm:sharp}
For every $M\in\CC^{2\times2}$ we have $2\lvert\det M\rvert\le\Fro{M}^2$. Consequently every
normalized state satisfies $C(M)\le1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Corollary~\ref{cor:hadamard} gives $\lvert\det M\rvert\le\lVert r_0\rVert\lVert r_1\rVert$, and
AM--GM gives $2\lVert r_0\rVert\lVert r_1\rVert\le\lVert r_0\rVert^2+\lVert r_1\rVert^2=\Fro{M}^2$
by Lemma~\ref{lem:rows}.
\end{proof}

\section{The row classification}

\begin{theorem}[Row classification]\label{thm:rowclass}
Let $M$ be a sharp maximizer. Then $\lVert r_0\rVert^2=\lVert r_1\rVert^2=\tfrac12$ and
$\ip{r_0}{r_1}=0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Normalization gives $x+y=1$ for $x=\lVert r_0\rVert^2$, $y=\lVert r_1\rVert^2$, and $C=1$ gives
$\lvert\det M\rvert^2=\tfrac14$. Substituting into \eqref{eq:gram},
$\lvert\ip{r_0}{r_1}\rvert^2+\tfrac14 = xy$. But $4xy=(x+y)^2-(x-y)^2=1-(x-y)^2\le1$, so
$\lvert\ip{r_0}{r_1}\rvert^2 = xy-\tfrac14\le 0$, forcing simultaneously $\ip{r_0}{r_1}=0$ and
$x=y=\tfrac12$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Maximally mixed marginal]\label{thm:mixed}
If $M$ is a sharp maximizer then $MM^{\dagger}=\tfrac12\Id$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The entries of $MM^{\dagger}$ are $\lVert r_0\rVert^2$, $\ip{r_0}{r_1}$, $\overline{\ip{r_0}{r_1}}$
and $\lVert r_1\rVert^2$; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:rowclass}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Marginal criterion]\label{thm:iff}
$M$ is a sharp maximizer if and only if $MM^{\dagger}=\tfrac12\Id$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Necessity is Theorem~\ref{thm:mixed}. Conversely, taking traces in $MM^{\dagger}=\tfrac12\Id$ and
using \eqref{eq:tracedet} gives $\Fro{M}^2=1$; taking determinants gives
$\lvert\det M\rvert^2=\det(\tfrac12\Id)=\tfrac14$, so $C(M)=1$.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:iff} is the physically striking form of the classification: a two-qubit pure state
is maximally entangled exactly when its one-qubit marginal is maximally mixed. Maximal global
correlation is maximal local ignorance.

\begin{theorem}[Unitary rescaling]\label{thm:unitary}
If $MM^{\dagger}=\tfrac12\Id$ then $\sqrt2\,M\in\Ut$. In particular $\Phi=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\Id$ is a
sharp maximizer.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$(\sqrt2M)(\sqrt2M)^{\dagger}=2MM^{\dagger}=\Id$. For $\Phi$, $\Phi\Phi^{\dagger}=\tfrac12\Id$, so
Theorem~\ref{thm:iff} applies.
\end{proof}

This is the step ``construct a unitary matrix from an orthonormal basis'': Theorem~\ref{thm:rowclass}
says the rows of $\sqrt2M$ are an orthonormal basis of $\CC^2$, and a matrix with orthonormal rows
\emph{is} unitary.

\section{The normal form theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Left transitivity]\label{thm:left}
$M$ is a sharp maximizer if and only if $M=U\Phi$ for some $U\in\Ut$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For necessity put $U=\sqrt2M$, unitary by Theorems~\ref{thm:mixed} and \ref{thm:unitary}; then
$U\Phi=M$. Sufficiency is Theorem~\ref{thm:inv} applied to the sharp maximizer $\Phi$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Local-unitary normal form]\label{thm:normalform}
$M$ is a sharp maximizer if and only if $M=U\Phi V^{\mathsf T}$ for some $U,V\in\Ut$. Equivalently,
the set of sharp maximizers is exactly the $\Ut\times\Ut$-orbit of $\Phi$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Necessity is Theorem~\ref{thm:left} with $V=\Id$; sufficiency is Theorem~\ref{thm:inv}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Right transitivity]
$M$ is a sharp maximizer if and only if $M=\Phi V^{\mathsf T}$ for some $V\in\Ut$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\Phi$ is scalar, hence central. Given a sharp maximizer, Theorem~\ref{thm:left} yields $U$ with
$M=U\Phi=\Phi U$; take $V=U^{\mathsf T}$, unitary by Lemma~\ref{lem:closure}, so $V^{\mathsf T}=U$.
The converse is Theorem~\ref{thm:inv}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Transitivity on the orbit]\label{cor:transitive}
If $M$ and $N$ are sharp maximizers then $N=WM$ for some $W\in\Ut$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Write $M=A\Phi$, $N=B\Phi$ with $A,B$ unitary and set $W=BA^{\dagger}$; then
$WM=BA^{\dagger}A\Phi=B\Phi=N$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Stabilizer of the Bell state]\label{thm:stab}
Let $U\in\Ut$ and let $V$ be any matrix. Then $U\Phi V^{\mathsf T}=\Phi$ if and only if
$V=\overline U:=(U^{\dagger})^{\mathsf T}$. Hence the stabilizer of $\Phi$ in $\Ut\times\Ut$ is
$\{(U,\overline U):U\in\Ut\}$, a copy of $\Ut$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Since $\Phi=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\Id$ is scalar, $U\Phi V^{\mathsf T}=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}UV^{\mathsf T}$, so
the equation is equivalent to $UV^{\mathsf T}=\Id$. Multiplying on the left by $U^{\dagger}$ gives
$V^{\mathsf T}=U^{\dagger}$, i.e.\ $V=\overline U$; conversely $UV^{\mathsf T}=UU^{\dagger}=\Id$.
\end{proof}

Thus the orbit is $(\Ut\times\Ut)/\Ut$, of real dimension $4+4-4=4$: the maximizers form a
four-real-dimensional family of matrices inside the seven-sphere of normalized states.

\begin{corollary}
A sharp maximizer is never a product state.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Product states have $C=0$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:product}, maximizers have $C=1$.
\end{proof}

\section{Flat maximizers and complex Hadamard matrices of order two}

\begin{definition}
$M$ is \emph{flat} if $\lvert m_{ij}\rvert=\tfrac12$ for all $i,j$. We write
$F_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ for the order-two Fourier (Hadamard) matrix.
\end{definition}

A flat sharp maximizer, rescaled by $2$, is exactly a \emph{complex Hadamard matrix} of order two: a
matrix with unimodular entries and pairwise orthogonal rows.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:diagunit}
If $\lvert d_0\rvert=\lvert d_1\rvert=1$ then $\diag(d)$ is unitary. Moreover $\tfrac12F_2$ is a
flat sharp maximizer.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$\diag(d)\diag(d)^{\dagger}=\diag(\lvert d_0\rvert^2,\lvert d_1\rvert^2)=\Id$. For $F_2$,
$(\tfrac12F_2)(\tfrac12F_2)^{\dagger}=\tfrac14F_2F_2^{\mathsf T}=\tfrac12\Id$, so
Theorem~\ref{thm:iff} applies; flatness is immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Dephasing]\label{thm:dephase}
Let $M$ be a flat sharp maximizer. Then there are unimodular $d,e\in\CC^2$ with
$M=\diag(d)\,\bigl(\tfrac12F_2\bigr)\,\diag(e)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Flatness gives $m_{ij}\overline{m_{ij}}=\tfrac14$ for all $i,j$; in particular no entry vanishes.
Theorem~\ref{thm:rowclass} gives $m_{00}\overline{m_{10}}+m_{01}\overline{m_{11}}=0$; multiplying by
$4m_{10}m_{11}$ and substituting $4m_{10}\overline{m_{10}}=4m_{11}\overline{m_{11}}=1$ yields the
unconjugated relation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:flatrel}
  m_{00}m_{11}+m_{01}m_{10}=0.
\end{equation}
Take $d=(1,\,m_{10}/m_{00})$ and $e=(2m_{00},\,2m_{01})$, both unimodular by flatness. Then
$\diag(d)(\tfrac12F_2)\diag(e)$ equals
$\begin{pmatrix}m_{00}&m_{01}\\ m_{10}&-m_{01}m_{10}/m_{00}\end{pmatrix}$, whose bottom-right entry
is $m_{11}$ precisely by \eqref{eq:flatrel}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Flat classification]
$M$ is a flat sharp maximizer if and only if $M=\diag(d)(\tfrac12F_2)\diag(e)$ for unimodular
$d,e$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Necessity is Theorem~\ref{thm:dephase}. For sufficiency, sharpness follows from
Lemma~\ref{lem:diagunit} and Theorem~\ref{thm:inv} (note $\diag(e)=\diag(e)^{\mathsf T}$, so this is
a legitimate local action), and flatness from the entrywise formula: each entry is
$\pm\tfrac12 d_ie_j$.
\end{proof}

This is the order-two case of the classification of complex Hadamard matrices, and it is a
\emph{rigidity} statement: whereas the full maximizer set requires the six-parameter group
$\Ut\times\Ut$ (modulo stabilizer) to sweep out, the flat locus requires only the three-parameter
torus of diagonal phases. There is no continuous family of order-two complex Hadamard matrices
beyond dephasing --- the \emph{defect} is zero. Contrast order four, which carries a genuine
one-parameter family.

\subsection{The real count}

\begin{theorem}[Sign criterion]\label{thm:signcrit}
Let $S(a,b,c,d)$ be the matrix with entries $\pm\tfrac12$ according to signs $a,b,c,d\in\{\pm\}$.
Then $S(a,b,c,d)$ is a sharp maximizer if and only if the propositions ``$a=d$'' and ``$b=c$'' have
opposite truth values.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Every such matrix is normalized, since $4\cdot\tfrac14=1$. Its determinant is $\tfrac14(ad-bc)$ with
$ad,bc\in\{\pm1\}$, so $\lvert\det\rvert=\tfrac12$ iff $ad=-bc$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The count]
Exactly $8$ of the $16$ real sign patterns are sharp maximizers.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The map $(a,b,c,d)\mapsto(a,b,c,-d)$ is a fixed-point-free involution exchanging maximizers with
non-maximizers, so the two classes have equal size.
\end{proof}

Equivalently, the eight real maximizers form a single orbit of the sign group $\{\pm1\}^3$ (row and
column signs modulo the global sign) through $\tfrac12F_2$ --- the real shadow of the flat
classification.

\section{The Bell basis}

Define the Hilbert--Schmidt inner product $\ip{M}{N}_{\HS}=\sum_{i,j}\overline{m_{ij}}n_{ij}$, which
is the standard inner product of the corresponding state vectors. Let $\sigma_0=\Id$ and
\[
  \sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
  \sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
  \sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},
\]
and set $\Phi_k=\sigma_k\Phi=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\sigma_k$.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:pauli}
Each $\sigma_k$ is unitary and $\ip{\sigma_j}{\sigma_k}_{\HS}=2\delta_{jk}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Direct computation: each $\sigma_k$ is Hermitian with $\sigma_k^2=\Id$, and the four are pairwise
Hilbert--Schmidt orthogonal with squared norm $\tr(\sigma_k^2)=2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Bell basis]\label{thm:bellbasis}
The four states $\Phi_0,\Phi_x,\Phi_y,\Phi_z$ are sharp maximizers, are orthonormal for
$\ip{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\HS}$, and form a basis: every amplitude matrix satisfies
\[
  M \;=\; \sum_k \ip{\Phi_k}{M}_{\HS}\;\Phi_k .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Sharpness: $\Phi_k=\Lambda_{\sigma_k,\Id}(\Phi)$ with $\sigma_k$ unitary, so Theorem~\ref{thm:inv}
applies. Orthonormality: $\ip{\Phi_j}{\Phi_k}_{\HS}=\tfrac12\ip{\sigma_j}{\sigma_k}_{\HS}
=\delta_{jk}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli}. Completeness: the Pauli matrices span $\CC^{2\times2}$ with
$M=\tfrac12\sum_k\ip{\sigma_k}{M}_{\HS}\sigma_k$ (verify entrywise, or use orthogonality plus a
dimension count); substituting $\sigma_k=\sqrt2\Phi_k$ and
$\ip{\sigma_k}{M}_{\HS}=\sqrt2\ip{\Phi_k}{M}_{\HS}$ gives the stated formula.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:bellbasis} is the structural fact behind superdense coding and teleportation: there
is an orthonormal basis of the four-dimensional two-qubit state space consisting entirely of
maximally entangled states, whose members differ by a unitary acting on one side only.

\section{Purity, linear entropy, and the Schmidt spectrum}

Cayley--Hamilton in dimension two, $A^2-(\tr A)A+(\det A)\Id=0$, gives in trace form
$\tr(A^2)=(\tr A)^2-2\det A$. Applying this to $\rho=MM^{\dagger}$ with \eqref{eq:tracedet}:

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:purity}
$\tr\rho^2 = \Fro{M}^4 - 2\lvert\det M\rvert^2$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Linear-entropy identity]\label{thm:linent}
For every normalized $M$, $\;C(M)^2 = 2\bigl(1-\tr\rho^2\bigr)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $\Fro{M}^2=1$ into Proposition~\ref{prop:purity}: $\tr\rho^2=1-2\lvert\det M\rvert^2
=1-\tfrac12C^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Minimal purity]
Every normalized state has $\tr\rho^2\ge\tfrac12$, with equality exactly at the sharp maximizers.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
$\tr\rho^2=1-\tfrac12C^2\ge\tfrac12$ since $C\le1$, with equality iff $C=1$ (using $C\ge0$).
\end{proof}

\subsection{The Schmidt spectrum}

\begin{definition}
For a normalized state set $s_{\pm}(M)=\bigl(1\pm\sqrt{1-C(M)^2}\bigr)/2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:schmidt}
$s_++s_-=1$, $s_+s_-=\lvert\det M\rvert^2$ and $0\le s_-\le s_+\le1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The sum is immediate; $s_+s_-=\tfrac14\bigl(1-(1-C^2)\bigr)=\tfrac14C^2=\lvert\det M\rvert^2$, using
$C\le1$ so that $\bigl(\sqrt{1-C^2}\bigr)^2=1-C^2$. The bounds follow from
$0\le\sqrt{1-C^2}\le1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Schmidt spectrum]\label{thm:spectrum}
For a normalized state, $\bigl(\rho-s_+\Id\bigr)\bigl(\rho-s_-\Id\bigr)=0$; thus the eigenvalues of
the marginal --- the squared Schmidt coefficients of the state --- are exactly $s_{\pm}(M)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Expand as $\rho^2-(s_++s_-)\rho+s_+s_-\Id=\rho^2-(\tr\rho)\rho+(\det\rho)\Id$, using
Lemma~\ref{lem:schmidt} with $\tr\rho=1$ and $\det\rho=\lvert\det M\rvert^2$; this vanishes by
Cayley--Hamilton.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Both extremes as spectral degeneracies]
For a normalized state: $M$ is a sharp maximizer iff $s_+=s_-$ (spectrum $\{\tfrac12,\tfrac12\}$),
and $M$ is a product state iff $s_-=0$ (spectrum $\{1,0\}$).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
$s_+-s_-=\sqrt{1-C^2}$ vanishes iff $C=1$; and $2s_-=1-\sqrt{1-C^2}$ vanishes iff $C=0$, which by
Theorem~\ref{thm:product} is the product condition.
\end{proof}

\section{Stability: a quantitative inverse theorem}

The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:rowclass} discarded a non-negative term; retaining it turns the
classification into an exact identity, hence into a robust statement.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:margexp}
For every $M$, with $\rho=MM^{\dagger}$,
\[
  \Fro{\rho-\tfrac12\Id}^2
   = \bigl(\lVert r_0\rVert^2-\tfrac12\bigr)^2 + \bigl(\lVert r_1\rVert^2-\tfrac12\bigr)^2
     + 2\lvert\ip{r_0}{r_1}\rvert^2 .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The entries of $\rho$ are $\rho_{00}=\lVert r_0\rVert^2$, $\rho_{11}=\lVert r_1\rVert^2$,
$\rho_{01}=\ip{r_0}{r_1}$, $\rho_{10}=\overline{\rho_{01}}$; subtract $\tfrac12\Id$ and sum the four
squared moduli.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact stability identity]\label{thm:stability}
For every normalized $M$,
\[
  \Fro{\,MM^{\dagger}-\tfrac12\Id\,}^2 \;=\; \frac{1-C(M)^2}{2}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $x=\lVert r_0\rVert^2$, $y=\lVert r_1\rVert^2$, $t=\lvert\ip{r_0}{r_1}\rvert^2$ and
$D=\lvert\det M\rvert^2=C^2/4$. Normalization gives $x+y=1$ and \eqref{eq:gram} gives $t+D=xy$.
Then
\[
  \bigl(x-\tfrac12\bigr)^2+\bigl(y-\tfrac12\bigr)^2=\tfrac12(x-y)^2
   =\tfrac12\bigl((x+y)^2-4xy\bigr)=\tfrac12\bigl(1-4t-4D\bigr),
\]
so by Lemma~\ref{lem:margexp} the quantity equals $\tfrac12-2t-2D+2t=\tfrac12-\tfrac{C^2}{2}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Deficit bound]\label{cor:deficit}
For every normalized $M$, $\;\Fro{MM^{\dagger}-\tfrac12\Id}^2\le 1-C(M)$, and the left side vanishes
if and only if $M$ is a sharp maximizer.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
$\tfrac12(1-C^2)=\tfrac12(1-C)(1+C)\le 1-C$ since $0\le C\le1$; vanishing is equivalent to $C=1$.
\end{proof}

Thus a state whose concurrence falls short of the maximum by $\varepsilon$ has a marginal within
Frobenius distance $\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ of maximally mixed, and the exponent is optimal by the exact
identity. The classification is not a knife-edge phenomenon: it degrades continuously with an
explicit modulus.

\section{Algorithmic content}

Every theorem above supplies an explicit witness; each of the following runs in $O(1)$ arithmetic
operations because the dimension is fixed.

\begin{itemize}
\item[\textbf{A}] \emph{Certify maximality.} Compute $\Fro{M}^2$ and $\det M$; report ``sharp
  maximizer'' iff $\Fro{M}^2=1$ and $2\lvert\det M\rvert=1$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:iff} this is
  equivalent to the four-entry test $MM^{\dagger}=\tfrac12\Id$, which is what one measures
  experimentally by tomography of a single qubit.
\item[\textbf{B}] \emph{Normal-form extraction.} For a sharp maximizer return $U=\sqrt2M$, $V=\Id$;
  then $M=U\Phi V^{\mathsf T}$ with $U$ unitary (Theorem~\ref{thm:unitary}).
\item[\textbf{C}] \emph{Interconversion.} For sharp maximizers $M,N$ return $W=2NM^{\dagger}$; then
  $W$ is unitary and $WM=N$, realizing Corollary~\ref{cor:transitive} explicitly.
\item[\textbf{D}] \emph{Dephasing.} For a flat sharp maximizer return $d=(1,m_{10}/m_{00})$ and
  $e=(2m_{00},2m_{01})$, so that $M=\diag(d)(\tfrac12F_2)\diag(e)$.
\item[\textbf{E}] \emph{Bell-basis transform.} Return $c_k=\ip{\Phi_k}{M}_{\HS}
  =\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\tr(\sigma_k^{\dagger}M)$; then $M=\sum_kc_k\Phi_k$ and
  $\sum_k\lvert c_k\rvert^2=\Fro{M}^2$.
\item[\textbf{F}] \emph{Schmidt spectrum.} Return $s_{\pm}=\bigl(1\pm\sqrt{1-C^2}\bigr)/2$ with
  $C=2\lvert\det M\rvert$; these are the eigenvalues of $MM^{\dagger}$, obtained without
  diagonalizing anything.
\end{itemize}

\section{Discussion}

\subsection*{Entanglement as an extremal problem}
The narrative is a template. A sharp inequality is proved by dropping one non-negative term and
applying AM--GM; the equality case reinstates both, forcing two equations; those equations assemble
into a matrix identity ($\rho=\tfrac12\Id$); the matrix identity says the object is unitary after
rescaling; and unitarity is precisely membership in a group orbit. Wherever this template applies
--- Hadamard matrices, tight frames, extremal graphs, isoperimetric problems --- one expects the
maximizer set to be a single orbit, and the proof of the inequality, read backwards, to be the
classification.

\subsection*{Operational content}
Theorem~\ref{thm:iff} says maximal entanglement is exactly maximal local ignorance, which is why the
halves of a Bell pair are individually useless: each is a uniformly random bit.
Corollary~\ref{cor:transitive} says either party can convert their shared maximally entangled state
into any other by acting alone, which is why ``maximally entangled state'' is a resource without
further qualification. Theorem~\ref{thm:stab} explains the isotropy of Bell correlations: rotating
one particle by $U$ can always be undone by rotating the other by $\overline U$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:bellbasis} is the mathematical substrate of superdense coding and teleportation.

\subsection*{Combinatorial content}
The flat classification and the count place the analysis in contact with the combinatorics of
Hadamard matrices. Order two is the base case of a hierarchy that becomes hard fast --- the
classification of complex Hadamard matrices is complete only up to order five. What the base case
exhibits cleanly is \emph{defect zero}: the only deformations of $F_2$ through complex Hadamard
matrices are the trivial ones by row and column phases. The count $8=\lvert\{\pm1\}^3\rvert$ is its
exact discrete shadow.

\subsection*{Stability}
Theorem~\ref{thm:stability} upgrades a rigidity theorem to a robustness theorem. In an experiment one
never certifies $C=1$ but only $C\ge1-\varepsilon$; Corollary~\ref{cor:deficit} converts that
certificate directly into a bound on how far the observed one-qubit marginal can be from maximally
mixed, with no free constants.

\section{Future directions}

\subsection*{Direction 1: a complete local-unitary invariant via the Schmidt normal form}
The row classification is the equality case of a Gram inequality whose general case is the singular
value decomposition. The same Lagrange identity that produced $MM^{\dagger}=\tfrac12\Id$ should
produce the general normal form $M=U\diag(s,t)V^{\mathsf T}$, exhibiting the Schmidt coefficients as
a complete invariant of the local action on \emph{all} states, not only the maximizers. The
ingredients are in place: $MM^{\dagger}$ is Hermitian positive semidefinite with spectrum computed
in Theorem~\ref{thm:spectrum}, the degenerate cases in dimension two are a finite check, and the
orbit machinery already applies. The expected conclusion --- that two states are locally equivalent
iff they have the same concurrence --- would place the whole development inside one classification.

\subsection*{Direction 2: the Hadamard defect and the rigidity of $F_2$}
Theorem~\ref{thm:dephase} shows the order-two complex Hadamard matrices admit exactly a
three-parameter dephasing group and no continuous family beyond it, i.e.\ defect zero, whereas order
four carries a genuine one-parameter family. A formal notion of \emph{defect} --- the dimension of
the space of infinitesimal deformations preserving unimodularity and orthogonality, modulo dephasing
--- would explain both facts uniformly, and the order-two case now provides a fully proved base case
against which to calibrate the definition rather than folklore.

\subsection*{Direction 3: sharpness stability, from marginal to state}
The equality-case argument only ever used $\lvert\ip{r_0}{r_1}\rvert^2\le\varepsilon$, so it is
already quantitative: one expects $\Fro{M}^2-2\lvert\det M\rvert\le\varepsilon$ to force $M$ within
Frobenius distance $O(\sqrt\varepsilon)$ of the maximizer orbit. Theorem~\ref{thm:stability}
supplies the marginal-level half exactly. What remains is the passage from ``marginal close to
$\tfrac12\Id$'' to ``state close to the orbit'', i.e.\ a perturbative version of
Theorem~\ref{thm:unitary}: if $MM^{\dagger}$ is within $\delta$ of $\tfrac12\Id$ then $\sqrt2M$ is
within $O(\delta)$ of a unitary --- a two-dimensional instance of the problem of approximating
almost-unitary matrices by unitary ones, where the polar decomposition should give the optimal
constant.

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
from typing import Iterator, Tuple

import numpy as np

TOL: float = 1e-10
Matrix = np.ndarray

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic objects
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

SQRT2: float = float(np.sqrt(2.0))
PHI: Matrix = np.eye(2, dtype=complex) / SQRT2                 # the Bell state
F2: Matrix = np.array([[1, 1], [1, -1]], dtype=complex)        # Fourier / Hadamard
SIGMA = {
    "I": np.eye(2, dtype=complex),
    "X": np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]], dtype=complex),
    "Y": np.array([[0, -1j], [1j, 0]], dtype=complex),
    "Z": np.array([[1, 0], [0, -1]], dtype=complex),
}


def frob_sq(M: Matrix) -> float:
    """Squared Frobenius norm = total probability of the state."""
    return float(np.sum(np.abs(M) ** 2))


def concurrence(M: Matrix) -> float:
    """Wootters concurrence C(M) = 2 |det M|."""
    return float(2.0 * abs(np.linalg.det(M)))


def marginal(M: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """Reduced density matrix rho = M M^H of the first qubit."""
    return M @ M.conj().T


def purity(M: Matrix) -> float:
    """tr(rho^2) for rho = M M^H."""
    rho = marginal(M)
    return float(np.real(np.trace(rho @ rho)))


def is_normalized(M: Matrix) -> bool:
    return abs(frob_sq(M) - 1.0) < TOL


def is_sharp_maximizer(M: Matrix) -> bool:
    """Algorithm A: certify maximality in O(1) operations."""
    return is_normalized(M) and abs(concurrence(M) - 1.0) < TOL


def is_unitary(U: Matrix) -> bool:
    return bool(np.allclose(U @ U.conj().T, np.eye(2), atol=1e-9))


def is_flat(M: Matrix) -> bool:
    return bool(np.allclose(np.abs(M), 0.5, atol=1e-9))


def local_act(U: Matrix, V: Matrix, M: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """The local action of U (x) V on amplitude matrices: M -> U M V^T."""
    return U @ M @ V.T


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Random generators
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def random_unitary(rng: np.random.Generator) -> Matrix:
    """Haar-distributed 2x2 unitary via QR of a complex Ginibre matrix."""
    z = (rng.normal(size=(2, 2)) + 1j * rng.normal(size=(2, 2))) / np.sqrt(2.0)
    q, r = np.linalg.qr(z)
    return q @ np.diag(np.diag(r) / np.abs(np.diag(r)))


def random_state(rng: np.random.Generator) -> Matrix:
    """A uniformly random normalized amplitude matrix."""
    z = rng.normal(size=(2, 2)) + 1j * rng.normal(size=(2, 2))
    return z / np.sqrt(frob_sq(z))


def random_maximizer(rng: np.random.Generator) -> Matrix:
    """A random maximally entangled state: U Phi V^T with Haar U, V."""
    return local_act(random_unitary(rng), random_unitary(rng), PHI)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Algorithms extracted from the theorems
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def normal_form(M: Matrix) -> Tuple[Matrix, Matrix]:
    """Algorithm B. For a sharp maximizer return (U, V) with M = U Phi V^T."""
    if not is_sharp_maximizer(M):
        raise ValueError("normal_form requires a sharp maximizer")
    return SQRT2 * M, np.eye(2, dtype=complex)


def interconvert(M: Matrix, N: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """Algorithm C. For maximizers M, N return the unitary W with W M = N."""
    return 2.0 * N @ M.conj().T


def dephase_flat(M: Matrix) -> Tuple[Matrix, Matrix]:
    """Algorithm D. For a flat maximizer return diagonal unitaries (D, E)
    with M = D (F2 / 2) E."""
    d = np.array([1.0 + 0j, M[1, 0] / M[0, 0]])
    e = np.array([2.0 * M[0, 0], 2.0 * M[0, 1]])
    return np.diag(d), np.diag(e)


def bell_basis() -> list[Matrix]:
    """The Pauli orbit of the Bell state: an orthonormal basis of maximizers."""
    return [SIGMA[k] / SQRT2 for k in ("I", "X", "Y", "Z")]


def hs_inner(M: Matrix, N: Matrix) -> complex:
    """Hilbert-Schmidt inner product <M, N> = sum conj(M_ij) N_ij."""
    return complex(np.sum(np.conj(M) * N))


def bell_coefficients(M: Matrix) -> np.ndarray:
    """Algorithm E. Coefficients of M in the Bell basis."""
    return np.array([hs_inner(B, M) for B in bell_basis()])


def schmidt_spectrum(M: Matrix) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Algorithm F. The eigenvalues (1 +- sqrt(1 - C^2)) / 2 of the marginal."""
    c = concurrence(M)
    root = float(np.sqrt(max(0.0, 1.0 - c * c)))
    return (1.0 + root) / 2.0, (1.0 - root) / 2.0

def banner(title: str) -> None:
    print("\n" + "=" * 74)

def demo_sharp_bound(rng: np.random.Generator, trials: int = 200_000) -> None:
    banner("1. Sharp bound  2 |det M| <= ||M||_F^2  and  C <= 1 on normalized states")
    worst = 0.0
    best_c = 0.0
    for _ in range(trials // 1000):
        z = rng.normal(size=(2, 2)) + 1j * rng.normal(size=(2, 2))
        slack = frob_sq(z) - 2.0 * abs(np.linalg.det(z))
        worst = min(worst, slack)
        best_c = max(best_c, concurrence(random_state(rng)))
    print(f"  minimum observed slack ||M||_F^2 - 2|det M| : {worst:+.12f}   (must be >= 0)")
    print(f"  largest concurrence among random states     : {best_c:.6f}   (<= 1)")
    print(f"  concurrence of the Bell state Phi           : {concurrence(PHI):.12f}")
    print(f"  equality holds for Phi, so the bound is sharp.")

    print(f"  ||row0||^2 = {frob_sq(M[0]):.12f}   ||row1||^2 = {frob_sq(M[1]):.12f}   (both 1/2)")
    print(f"  <row0, row1> = {np.vdot(M[1], M[0]):+.2e}   (zero)")
    print("  rho = M M^H =")
    print(np.array2string(rho, precision=6, suppress_small=True, prefix="    "))
    print(f"  ||rho - I/2||_F = {np.sqrt(frob_sq(rho - np.eye(2) / 2)):.2e}")
    print(f"  sqrt(2) M is unitary : {is_unitary(SQRT2 * M)}")
    print("\n  Converse check: a matrix with maximally mixed marginal is a maximizer.")
    U = random_unitary(rng)
    N = U / SQRT2
    print(f"    N = U/sqrt2 with U Haar-random -> is_sharp_maximizer(N) = {is_sharp_maximizer(N)}")


def demo_normal_form(rng: np.random.Generator) -> None:
    banner("4-5. Normal form, one-sided transitivity and explicit interconversion")
    M = random_maximizer(rng)
    U, V = normal_form(M)
    print(f"  extracted U unitary : {is_unitary(U)}")
    print(f"  || M - U Phi V^T ||  = {np.sqrt(frob_sq(M - local_act(U, V, PHI))):.2e}")
    print("  (the right factor is the identity: the LEFT action alone is transitive)")

    N = random_maximizer(rng)

    print(f"  || N - W M ||          = {np.sqrt(frob_sq(N - W @ M)):.2e}")
    print("  so one party, acting on their qubit alone, converts any maximizer into any other.")

    R = random_state(rng)
    A, B = random_unitary(rng), random_unitary(rng)
    RA = local_act(A, B, R)
    print(f"    ||R||_F^2 = {frob_sq(R):.10f}  ->  {frob_sq(RA):.10f}")
    print(f"    C(R)      = {concurrence(R):.10f}  ->  {concurrence(RA):.10f}")

    U = random_unitary(rng)

          "   (generically nonzero)")

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
from typing import Iterator, Tuple

import numpy as np

TOL: float = 1e-10
Matrix = np.ndarray

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic objects
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

SQRT2: float = float(np.sqrt(2.0))
PHI: Matrix = np.eye(2, dtype=complex) / SQRT2                 # the Bell state
F2: Matrix = np.array([[1, 1], [1, -1]], dtype=complex)        # Fourier / Hadamard
SIGMA = {
    "I": np.eye(2, dtype=complex),
    "X": np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]], dtype=complex),
    "Y": np.array([[0, -1j], [1j, 0]], dtype=complex),
    "Z": np.array([[1, 0], [0, -1]], dtype=complex),
}


def frob_sq(M: Matrix) -> float:
    """Squared Frobenius norm = total probability of the state."""
    return float(np.sum(np.abs(M) ** 2))


def concurrence(M: Matrix) -> float:
    """Wootters concurrence C(M) = 2 |det M|."""
    return float(2.0 * abs(np.linalg.det(M)))


def marginal(M: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """Reduced density matrix rho = M M^H of the first qubit."""
    return M @ M.conj().T


def purity(M: Matrix) -> float:
    """tr(rho^2) for rho = M M^H."""
    rho = marginal(M)
    return float(np.real(np.trace(rho @ rho)))


def is_normalized(M: Matrix) -> bool:
    return abs(frob_sq(M) - 1.0) < TOL


def is_sharp_maximizer(M: Matrix) -> bool:
    """Algorithm A: certify maximality in O(1) operations."""
    return is_normalized(M) and abs(concurrence(M) - 1.0) < TOL


def is_unitary(U: Matrix) -> bool:
    return bool(np.allclose(U @ U.conj().T, np.eye(2), atol=1e-9))


def is_flat(M: Matrix) -> bool:
    return bool(np.allclose(np.abs(M), 0.5, atol=1e-9))


def local_act(U: Matrix, V: Matrix, M: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """The local action of U (x) V on amplitude matrices: M -> U M V^T."""
    return U @ M @ V.T


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Random generators
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def random_unitary(rng: np.random.Generator) -> Matrix:
    """Haar-distributed 2x2 unitary via QR of a complex Ginibre matrix."""
    z = (rng.normal(size=(2, 2)) + 1j * rng.normal(size=(2, 2))) / np.sqrt(2.0)
    q, r = np.linalg.qr(z)
    return q @ np.diag(np.diag(r) / np.abs(np.diag(r)))


def random_state(rng: np.random.Generator) -> Matrix:
    """A uniformly random normalized amplitude matrix."""
    z = rng.normal(size=(2, 2)) + 1j * rng.normal(size=(2, 2))
    return z / np.sqrt(frob_sq(z))


def random_maximizer(rng: np.random.Generator) -> Matrix:
    """A random maximally entangled state: U Phi V^T with Haar U, V."""
    return local_act(random_unitary(rng), random_unitary(rng), PHI)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Algorithms extracted from the theorems
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def normal_form(M: Matrix) -> Tuple[Matrix, Matrix]:
    """Algorithm B. For a sharp maximizer return (U, V) with M = U Phi V^T."""
    if not is_sharp_maximizer(M):
        raise ValueError("normal_form requires a sharp maximizer")
    return SQRT2 * M, np.eye(2, dtype=complex)


def interconvert(M: Matrix, N: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """Algorithm C. For maximizers M, N return the unitary W with W M = N."""
    return 2.0 * N @ M.conj().T


def dephase_flat(M: Matrix) -> Tuple[Matrix, Matrix]:
    """Algorithm D. For a flat maximizer return diagonal unitaries (D, E)
    with M = D (F2 / 2) E."""
    d = np.array([1.0 + 0j, M[1, 0] / M[0, 0]])
    e = np.array([2.0 * M[0, 0], 2.0 * M[0, 1]])
    return np.diag(d), np.diag(e)


def bell_basis() -> list[Matrix]:
    """The Pauli orbit of the Bell state: an orthonormal basis of maximizers."""
    return [SIGMA[k] / SQRT2 for k in ("I", "X", "Y", "Z")]


def hs_inner(M: Matrix, N: Matrix) -> complex:
    """Hilbert-Schmidt inner product <M, N> = sum conj(M_ij) N_ij."""
    return complex(np.sum(np.conj(M) * N))


def bell_coefficients(M: Matrix) -> np.ndarray:
    """Algorithm E. Coefficients of M in the Bell basis."""
    return np.array([hs_inner(B, M) for B in bell_basis()])


def schmidt_spectrum(M: Matrix) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Algorithm F. The eigenvalues (1 +- sqrt(1 - C^2)) / 2 of the marginal."""
    c = concurrence(M)
    root = float(np.sqrt(max(0.0, 1.0 - c * c)))
    return (1.0 + root) / 2.0, (1.0 - root) / 2.0

        slack = frob_sq(z) - 2.0 * abs(np.linalg.det(z))

def haar_unitaries(n: int, rng: np.random.Generator) -> np.ndarray:
    """n Haar-random 2x2 unitaries, batched."""
    z = (rng.normal(size=(n, 2, 2)) + 1j * rng.normal(size=(n, 2, 2))) / np.sqrt(2.0)
    out = np.empty_like(z)
    for k in range(n):
        q, r = np.linalg.qr(z[k])
        out[k] = q @ np.diag(np.diag(r) / np.abs(np.diag(r)))
    return out

import numpy as np

SQRT2: float = float(np.sqrt(2.0))


def project_to_orbit(M: np.ndarray, iters: int = 60, tol: float = 1e-15) -> np.ndarray:
    """Return the maximally entangled state closest to M in Frobenius norm.

    Write the polar decomposition M = Q P with Q unitary and P positive
    semidefinite.  Because the maximizers are exactly the unitaries scaled by
    1/sqrt(2), the closest maximizer to M is Q / sqrt(2).  The unitary factor is
    computed by the quadratically convergent Newton iteration
    X <- (X + (X^H)^{-1}) / 2, which needs no eigendecomposition.

    X = np.array(M, dtype=complex)
    for _ in range(iters):

        Y = 0.5 * (X + np.linalg.inv(X.conj().T))
        if np.linalg.norm(Y - X) < tol:
            X = Y
            break
        X = Y
    return X / SQRT2

from typing import Tuple

import numpy as np

SQRT2: float = float(np.sqrt(2.0))
PAULI: np.ndarray = np.array([[[1, 0], [0, 1]], [[0, 1], [1, 0]],
                              [[0, -1j], [1j, 0]], [[1, 0], [0, -1]]], dtype=complex)
BELL: np.ndarray = PAULI / SQRT2       # the four Bell states, as amplitude matrices


def bell_transform(M: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Coefficients of M along the Bell basis: c_k = <Phi_k, M> (Hilbert-Schmidt)."""
    return np.array([complex(np.sum(np.conj(B) * M)) for B in BELL])


def bell_reconstruct(c: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Inverse transform: M = sum_k c_k Phi_k."""
    return sum(ck * B for ck, B in zip(c, BELL))


def schmidt_spectrum(M: np.ndarray) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Eigenvalues (1 +- sqrt(1 - C^2))/2 of the marginal M M^H, for normalized M.

    Obtained from the two invariants trace = 1 and determinant = |det M|^2 by
    Cayley-Hamilton; no eigendecomposition is performed.

    c = 2.0 * abs(complex(np.linalg.det(M)))
    root = float(np.sqrt(max(0.0, 1.0 - c * c)))
    return (1.0 + root) / 2.0, (1.0 - root) / 2.0

Three panels illustrating the local-unitary normal form.

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle

SQRT2: float = float(np.sqrt(2.0))
PHI: np.ndarray = np.eye(2, dtype=complex) / SQRT2


def concurrence(M: np.ndarray) -> float:
    return float(2.0 * abs(np.linalg.det(M)))


def su2(theta: float, phi: float, psi: float) -> np.ndarray:
    """A general SU(2) matrix in Euler form."""
    c, s = np.cos(theta / 2.0), np.sin(theta / 2.0)
    return np.array([[np.exp(1j * phi) * c, np.exp(1j * psi) * s],
                     [-np.exp(-1j * psi) * s, np.exp(-1j * phi) * c]], dtype=complex)


def panel_invariance(ax_amp: plt.Axes, ax_inv: plt.Axes) -> None:
    ts = np.linspace(0.0, 2.0 * np.pi, 600)
    amps = np.zeros((len(ts), 4))
    conc = np.zeros(len(ts))
    dist = np.zeros(len(ts))
    for k, t in enumerate(ts):
        U = su2(t, 0.7 * t, 0.3 * t)
        V = su2(0.6 * t, -0.4 * t, 1.1 * t)
        M = U @ PHI @ V.T
        amps[k] = np.abs(M).reshape(4) ** 2
        conc[k] = concurrence(M)
        rho = M @ M.conj().T
        dist[k] = float(np.sum(np.abs(rho - np.eye(2) / 2.0) ** 2))
    labels = ["$|m_{00}|^2$", "$|m_{01}|^2$", "$|m_{10}|^2$", "$|m_{11}|^2$"]
    styles = ["-", "--", "-", "--"]
    for j in range(4):
        ax_amp.plot(ts, amps[:, j], lw=1.8, ls=styles[j], label=labels[j])
    ax_amp.set_xlabel("local-rotation parameter $t$")
    ax_amp.set_ylabel("outcome probabilities")
    ax_amp.set_title("(a) the amplitudes move ...")
    ax_amp.legend(fontsize=8, ncol=2)
    ax_amp.grid(alpha=0.25)

    ax_inv.plot(ts, conc, lw=2.4, color="#cc2222", label="concurrence $C$")
    ax_inv.plot(ts, 1e6 * dist + 0.5, lw=1.4, color="#2a8a5a",
                label=r"$10^6\|\rho-\frac{1}{2}I\|_F^2 + 0.5$")
    ax_inv.set_ylim(0.0, 1.2)
    ax_inv.set_xlabel("local-rotation parameter $t$")
    ax_inv.set_title("(b) ... the invariants do not")
    ax_inv.legend(fontsize=9, loc="lower right")
    ax_inv.grid(alpha=0.25)


def panel_stabilizer(ax: plt.Axes) -> None:
    rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
    theta0, phi0, psi0 = rng.uniform(0, np.pi), rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi), \
        rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi)
    U = su2(theta0, phi0, psi0)
    Ubar = U.conj()
    # conj(U) = su2(-theta0, -phi0, -psi0) up to the parametrization; scan a grid
    # in the two phase angles around the true conjugate.
    a = np.linspace(-np.pi, np.pi, 240)
    b = np.linspace(-np.pi, np.pi, 240)
    A, B = np.meshgrid(a, b, indexing="ij")
    Z = np.zeros_like(A)
    for i in range(A.shape[0]):
        for j in range(A.shape[1]):
            D = np.diag([np.exp(1j * A[i, j]), np.exp(1j * B[i, j])])
            V = D @ Ubar
            Z[i, j] = float(np.sqrt(np.sum(np.abs(U @ PHI @ V.T - PHI) ** 2)))
    im = ax.pcolormesh(A, B, Z, shading="auto", cmap="magma")
    ax.scatter([0.0], [0.0], s=90, facecolor="none", edgecolor="cyan", lw=2)
    ax.annotate(r"$V=\overline{U}$", (0.0, 0.0), textcoords="offset points",
                xytext=(10, 10), color="cyan", fontsize=12)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"phase $\alpha$ applied to $\overline{U}$")
    ax.set_ylabel(r"phase $\beta$ applied to $\overline{U}$")
    ax.set_title(r"(c) stabilizer: $\|U\Phi V^{T}-\Phi\|_F$ vanishes only at $V=\overline{U}$")
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046)


def panel_signs(ax: plt.Axes) -> None:
    ax.set_xlim(-0.4, 8.4)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.5, 4.3)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axis("off")
    for idx, signs in enumerate(itertools.product([1, -1], repeat=4)):
        a, b, c, d = signs
        S = np.array([[a, b], [c, d]], dtype=float) / 2.0
        sharp = abs(2 * abs(np.linalg.det(S)) - 1.0) < 1e-12
        col, row = idx % 8, idx // 8
        x0, y0 = col, 2.3 - 2.1 * row
        face = "#d9f0dd" if sharp else "#f6e2e2"
        edge = "#1f7a3d" if sharp else "#a33a3a"
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, y0), 0.9, 1.5, facecolor=face,
                               edgecolor=edge, lw=2.0))
        for (i, j), v in np.ndenumerate(np.array([[a, b], [c, d]])):
            ax.text(x0 + 0.25 + 0.42 * j, y0 + 1.05 - 0.60 * i,
                    "+" if v > 0 else "\u2212", ha="center", va="center",
                    fontsize=15, color=edge, fontweight="bold")
        ax.text(x0 + 0.45, y0 - 0.22, "max" if sharp else "no", ha="center",
                fontsize=9, color=edge)
    ax.set_title("(d) exactly 8 of the 16 real sign patterns are maximally entangled\n"
                 r"criterion: $(a=d)$ and $(b=c)$ must have opposite truth values",
                 fontsize=11)


def main() -> None:
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(15.5, 9.0))
    gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 3, height_ratios=[1.0, 1.05])
    ax_amp = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0])
    ax_inv = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1])
    ax_stab = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 2])
    ax_sign = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, :])
    panel_invariance(ax_amp, ax_inv)
    panel_stabilizer(ax_stab)
    panel_signs(ax_sign)
    fig.suptitle("One orbit, one stabilizer, eight sign patterns", fontsize=15)
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.96))
    fig.savefig("maximizer_orbit.png", dpi=155)
    print("wrote maximizer_orbit.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

<summary>Click to reveal the mathematics behind every readout</summary>
<p>
<b>Lagrange's identity.</b> For rows r<sub>0</sub> = (m<sub>00</sub>, m<sub>01</sub>) and
r<sub>1</sub> = (m<sub>10</sub>, m<sub>11</sub>),
|⟨r<sub>0</sub>, r<sub>1</sub>⟩|² + |det M|² = ‖r<sub>0</sub>‖²‖r<sub>1</sub>‖².
Discard the first term and apply the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality:
2|det M| ≤ 2‖r<sub>0</sub>‖‖r<sub>1</sub>‖ ≤ ‖r<sub>0</sub>‖² + ‖r<sub>1</sub>‖² = ‖M‖<sub>F</sub>².
So C ≤ 1 on normalized states.
</p>
<p>
<b>The equality case.</b> Equality in the second step forces the two row lengths to be equal, hence
½ each; equality in the first forces the rows to be orthogonal. Those four scalar statements
are exactly the four entries of ρ = I/2. Conversely, taking the trace and the determinant of
ρ = I/2 recovers normalization and |det M| = ½.
</p>
<p>
<b>Why "snap" works.</b> If ρ = I/2 then (√2 M)(√2 M)<sup>†</sup> = I, so √2 M is unitary
— a maximizer is nothing but a unitary matrix scaled by 1/√2. Hence the maximizers are
exactly {UΦ : U unitary} with Φ = diag(1/√2, 1/√2), the Bell state, and the nearest one
to a given M is obtained from the unitary factor of its polar decomposition.
</p>
<p>
<b>The stability identity.</b> Keeping the discarded term instead of throwing it away gives, for every
normalized state, the exact equality ‖ρ − I/2‖<sub>F</sub>² = (1 − C²)/2 ≤ 1 − C.
The two numbers in the table labelled "predicted" and "‖ρ − I/2‖<sub>F</sub>²" always agree
to machine precision — that is the identity being verified live.
</p>

<script>
const N = ["m00","m01","m10","m11"];
let st = N.map(()=>({r:0.5, th:0}));

function build(){
  const box = document.getElementById("sliders");
  box.innerHTML = "";
  N.forEach((nm,i)=>{
    const d = document.createElement("div");
    d.innerHTML =
      `<div class="amp"><label>|${nm}|</label>
        <input type="range" min="0" max="1" step="0.001" id="r${i}" value="${st[i].r}">
        <span class="val" id="rv${i}"></span></div>
       <div class="amp"><label>arg ${nm}</label>
        <input type="range" min="-3.1416" max="3.1416" step="0.01" id="t${i}" value="${st[i].th}">
        <span class="val" id="tv${i}"></span></div>`;
    box.appendChild(d);
  });
  N.forEach((nm,i)=>{
    document.getElementById("r"+i).addEventListener("input",e=>{st[i].r=+e.target.value;render();});
    document.getElementById("t"+i).addEventListener("input",e=>{st[i].th=+e.target.value;render();});
  });
}

function amps(){
  // complex amplitudes, then normalize
  let a = st.map(s=>[s.r*Math.cos(s.th), s.r*Math.sin(s.th)]);
  let n = Math.sqrt(a.reduce((s,z)=>s+z[0]*z[0]+z[1]*z[1],0));
  if(n < 1e-9){ a = [[1,0],[0,0],[0,0],[0,0]]; n = 1; }
  return a.map(z=>[z[0]/n, z[1]/n]);
}
const cmul=(x,y)=>[x[0]*y[0]-x[1]*y[1], x[0]*y[1]+x[1]*y[0]];
const csub=(x,y)=>[x[0]-y[0], x[1]-y[1]];
const cconj=x=>[x[0],-x[1]];
const cabs=x=>Math.hypot(x[0],x[1]);

function analyse(){
  const [a,b,c,d] = amps();
  const det = csub(cmul(a,d), cmul(b,c));
  const C = 2*cabs(det);
  const r0 = a[0]*a[0]+a[1]*a[1] + b[0]*b[0]+b[1]*b[1];
  const r1 = c[0]*c[0]+c[1]*c[1] + d[0]*d[0]+d[1]*d[1];
  const ip = [cmul(a,cconj(c))[0]+cmul(b,cconj(d))[0],
              cmul(a,cconj(c))[1]+cmul(b,cconj(d))[1]];
  const dist = (r0-0.5)*(r0-0.5) + (r1-0.5)*(r1-0.5) + 2*(ip[0]*ip[0]+ip[1]*ip[1]);
  const pur = 1 - C*C/2;
  const root = Math.sqrt(Math.max(0,1-C*C));
  return {a,b,c,d,det,C,r0,r1,ip,dist,pur,sp:(1+root)/2,sm:(1-root)/2};
}

function fmtC(z){ return (z[0]>=0?" ":"") + z[0].toFixed(4) + (z[1]>=0?" + ":" - ") + Math.abs(z[1]).toFixed(4) + "i"; }

function drawRho(A){
  const cv = document.getElementById("rhoCanvas"), g = cv.getContext("2d");
  g.clearRect(0,0,cv.width,cv.height);
  const vals = [
    ["\u03c1\u2080\u2080 = ||row\u2080||\u00b2", A.r0, "#5f7ff0"],
    ["\u03c1\u2081\u2081 = ||row\u2081||\u00b2", A.r1, "#37d67a"],
    ["|\u03c1\u2080\u2081| = |\u27e8row\u2080,row\u2081\u27e9|", Math.hypot(A.ip[0],A.ip[1]), "#ffb347"]
  ];
  const x0=190, w=cv.width-x0-24;
  vals.forEach((v,i)=>{
    const y = 34 + i*62;
    g.fillStyle="#93a0c8"; g.font="13px ui-monospace,monospace";
    g.fillText(v[0], 14, y+14);

};

<h1>The Local-Unitary Orbit Explorer</h1>
<p class="sub">
Start from the Bell state Φ = diag(1/√2, 1/√2) and rotate the two qubits independently:
M = U Φ V<sup>T</sup>. Both rotations are yours to choose. The four amplitudes and their phases will
churn wildly — and the concurrence will not move by so much as a rounding error. That is the
normal-form theorem made visible: <b>the maximally entangled states form a single orbit</b>, so you can
never leave it and you can always reach every point of it.
</p>

<div class="cols">
 <div>
  <div class="card">

      <button id="bReset">Reset to Φ</button>
      <button id="bRandU">Random U</button>
      <button id="bRandV">Random V</button>
    </div>
    <div class="note">
      Locking V to the entrywise conjugate of U puts you in the <b>stabilizer</b>: the state does not
      move at all, no matter how violently you turn U. Every other pair of rotations moves the state

    </div>
  </div>

    </table>
  </div>
 </div>

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal why the orbit is exactly the maximizer set</summary>
<p>
<b>Every maximizer is on the orbit.</b> If M is normalized with C(M) = 2|det M| = 1, then Lagrange's
identity forces the two rows of M to be orthogonal with squared length ½ each, i.e.
MM<sup>†</sup> = I/2. Hence (√2 M)(√2 M)<sup>†</sup> = I: the matrix U = √2 M is unitary,
and M = UΦ because Φ = I/√2. So one rotation of the <i>first</i> qubit alone already reaches M.
</p>
<p>
<b>Nothing else is on it.</b> Conversely, unitaries preserve the Frobenius norm and have unimodular
determinant, so C(UΦV<sup>T</sup>) = C(Φ) = 1 and the norm stays 1. The orbit is therefore exactly
the maximizer set.
</p>
<p>
<b>The stabilizer.</b> UΦV<sup>T</sup> = Φ is, after cancelling the scalar 1/√2, the equation
UV<sup>T</sup> = I, i.e. V<sup>T</sup> = U<sup>†</sup>, i.e. V is the entrywise conjugate of U. So the
stabilizer is a copy of the unitary group sitting diagonally-and-conjugately inside the product, and
the orbit has real dimension 4 + 4 − 4 = 4.
</p>
<p>
<b>Interconversion.</b> Given two maximizers M and N, the matrix W = 2NM<sup>†</sup> is unitary and
satisfies WM = N. One party, acting on one qubit, converts any maximally entangled state into any
other: there is really only one such state.
</p>
</details>

<script>
const cmul=(x,y)=>[x[0]*y[0]-x[1]*y[1], x[0]*y[1]+x[1]*y[0]];
const cadd=(x,y)=>[x[0]+y[0], x[1]+y[1]];
const csub=(x,y)=>[x[0]-y[0], x[1]-y[1]];
const cconj=x=>[x[0],-x[1]];
const cabs=x=>Math.hypot(x[0],x[1]);
const S = 1/Math.SQRT2;

let U = {th:0, ph:0, ps:0}, V = {th:0, ph:0, ps:0}, lock=false;
const hist = [];

function su2(p){
  const c=Math.cos(p.th/2), s=Math.sin(p.th/2);
  const e=(x)=>[Math.cos(x), Math.sin(x)];
  return [ cmul(e(p.ph),[c,0]), cmul(e(p.ps),[s,0]),
           cmul(e(-p.ps),[-s,0]), cmul(e(-p.ph),[c,0]) ];
}
function matmul(A,B){
  return [ cadd(cmul(A[0],B[0]),cmul(A[1],B[2])), cadd(cmul(A[0],B[1]),cmul(A[1],B[3])),
           cadd(cmul(A[2],B[0]),cmul(A[3],B[2])), cadd(cmul(A[2],B[1]),cmul(A[3],B[3])) ];
}
const transpose = A => [A[0],A[2],A[1],A[3]];
const conjM     = A => A.map(cconj);
const scale     = (A,k) => A.map(z=>[z[0]*k, z[1]*k]);

function state(){
  const Um = su2(U);
  const Vm = lock ? conjM(Um) : su2(V);
  return { M: scale(matmul(Um, transpose(Vm)), S), Um, Vm };
}

function analyse(M){
  const [a,b,c,d]=M;
  const det = csub(cmul(a,d), cmul(b,c));
  const C = 2*cabs(det);
  const F = M.reduce((s,z)=>s+z[0]*z[0]+z[1]*z[1],0);
  const r0 = a[0]*a[0]+a[1]*a[1]+b[0]*b[0]+b[1]*b[1];
  const r1 = c[0]*c[0]+c[1]*c[1]+d[0]*d[0]+d[1]*d[1];
  const ip = cadd(cmul(a,cconj(c)), cmul(b,cconj(d)));
  const dist = (r0-.5)**2 + (r1-.5)**2 + 2*(ip[0]**2+ip[1]**2);
  const bell = [[S,0],[0,0],[0,0],[S,0]];
  const pd = Math.sqrt(M.reduce((s,z,i)=>s+ (z[0]-bell[i][0])**2 + (z[1]-bell[i][1])**2, 0));
  return {C,F,dist,pd,r0,r1,ip};
}

function mkSliders(id, obj, tag){
  const names=[["th","\u03b8"],["ph","\u03c6"],["ps","\u03c8"]];
  const box=document.getElementById(id); box.innerHTML="";
  names.forEach(([k,sym])=>{
    const d=document.createElement("div"); d.className="sl";
    d.innerHTML=`<label>${sym}<sub>${tag}</sub></label>
      <input type="range" min="-3.1416" max="3.1416" step="0.005" id="${id}_${k}" value="${obj[k]}">
      <span class="val" id="${id}_${k}_v">${obj[k].toFixed(2)}</span>`;
    box.appendChild(d);
    d.querySelector("input").addEventListener("input", e=>{
      obj[k]=+e.target.value;
      document.getElementById(`${id}_${k}_v`).textContent=obj[k].toFixed(2);
      render();
    });
  });
}
function syncSliders(){
  [["uSliders",U],["vSliders",V]].forEach(([id,obj])=>{
    ["th","ph","ps"].forEach(k=>{
      const el=document.getElementById(`${id}_${k}`);
      if(el){ el.value=obj[k]; document.getElementById(`${id}_${k}_v`).textContent=obj[k].toFixed(2); }
    });
